summary:
Arecibo turns 25 years of NASA fire detections into one consistent record, then uses it to warn countries before a fire crisis and to show who can help.

NASA's two fire sensors, MODIS and VIIRS, cannot be compared directly: when VIIRS arrived in 2012, raw fire counts in Greece jumped 4.3 times with no more fires. We harmonize them (clean, match, count on one grid, calibrate month by month) and serve the result in a web app. Pick a country or draw an area, choose dates, and see a burning-activity calendar from 2001 to today, how the current month compares with its historical median, and a CSV download of the hotspots.

On that record we built two more tools. The Amber Index scores every EU country from 0 to 100, fire danger against firefighting readiness, and plans which countries can send help. A 3-day risk forecast, built from machine learning models trained on the harmonized fire record, adds NASA POWER weather, the Canadian Fire Weather Index, which tracks how dry the land has become, and the weather forecast for the days ahead. It estimates how much of each country will burn and raises an alert when that is unusual for the country.

Why it matters: in August 2025 Greece looked calm, then more than 100 wildfires broke out in a single day. The fire weather forecast had flagged that day a week ahead. Arecibo puts that warning in front of the people who decide.
details:
What it does

Arecibo is a web app built around one map of Europe.

Harmonized burning calendar. Click a country or draw your own area, pick a date range, and see fire activity by day, month and year from 2001 to today, in one unit that no longer depends on which satellite saw the fire. The app shows whether the current month is normal against its 2001 to 2020 median, lists the active fires, and exports every hotspot, the daily counts and the monthly calendar as CSV.

Amber Index. One score from 0 to 100 for every EU country and year: burned area and other hazards against firefighters, fire-protection spending and fire stations. A second number, firefighting power, shows how much capacity a country has left after the hazards it is already facing.

Who can help. Simulate a fire, flood, earthquake or heatwave in any country, and an optimizer splits a request for firefighters across the countries with power to spare, weighing distance against capacity. The plan is drawn as routes on the map.

Fire risk, up to 3 days ahead, for every map cell and every country.

How it works

Harmonization. We clean NASA FIRMS detections (vegetation fires only; low-confidence detections and fixed heat sources such as factories and flares are removed). A MODIS and a VIIRS detection within 1 km and 3 hours are treated as the same fire. Fires are counted as fire cell-days on a common grid, so pixel size (1 km against 375 m) stops mattering, and MODIS is calibrated to VIIRS month by month on the ten years both sensors flew. Tested by hiding one year at a time, the error on yearly totals is 4% for Romania and 7% for Greece. We also check detections against sources that do not use MODIS or VIIRS: ESA Sentinel-2 burn scars (dNBR) and Copernicus EMS rapid mapping.

Forecast. Our predictor is a set of LightGBM gradient-boosted tree models, trained only on days before a cutoff date. They take each cell's or patch's recent fire history, dryness, season and the next days' weather forecast. The cell model outputs the probability of a fire over the next 3 days. The country model uses a Poisson objective to output the expected number of burning cells on each of the next 1 to 3 days. Rare positives are handled by subsampling the negatives and re-weighting them. A time-based validation set picks the number of trees and each alert threshold, and the country risk is the sum over its patches.

Two models answer two questions: where (every 0.1 degree cell is scored every day) and how much (per country). The cell model gets plain physical quantities from NASA POWER (dry air, days since rain, 30-day rain, soil wetness, heat against normal, wind) instead of a ready-made fire index, so it learns that link itself. The country model adds the Canadian Fire Weather Index. A twin model with no fire history shows what weather alone can foresee.

We test on what the models never saw. The country model is trained up to 2024 and replayed on 2025 with ECMWF forecasts as issued. For the cell model, Greece's August 2025 is held out of training across Europe, then replayed, and leave-one-season-out cross-validation checks it across fire seasons. Both are compared with simple baselines such as persistence and the Fire Weather Index.

Impact

In August 2025 Greece, one of the best-staffed fire services in the EU per person, opened a request for EU help on 8 August and closed it because the situation had improved. Satellite fire activity that week was 88% below normal. On 12 August more than 100 wildfires broke out in one day. In western Achaia it was the most dangerous fire-weather day in 14 years of NASA record, and the weather forecast issued seven days earlier already ranked it in the top 2%. Going into that summer, the Amber Index had Greece as Red, second highest in the EU, with firefighting power of 35 out of 100. Arecibo cannot promise fewer fires. It can move the call for help a week earlier and point it at the countries able to answer.

What is creative, and what we considered

We go one step past the calendar the challenge asks for: from "what burned" to "who will need help, when, and who can give it".

We were strict about validation: only independent sources judge the detections, the forecast is replayed with the weather forecasts of the time, and each README lists the limits of its data.

MODIS is near the end of its life. The same calibration lets future sensors join the record.

Every view lives in the URL, so a link opens the same area, dates and panels for a colleague.

Tools

Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, LightGBM, SHAP, FastAPI, SQLite, Jupyter), JavaScript and TypeScript (React, Vite, Leaflet, MapLibre GL, D3), Sentinel-2 access through Microsoft Planetary Computer (pystac-client, odc-stac, rasterio), Git and GitHub.
